description_full: Aluminum Corporation of China Limited, together with its subsidiaries, primarily engages in the exploration and mining of bauxite, coal, and other resources in the People's Republic of China and internationally. It operates through five segments: Alumina, Primary Aluminum, Energy, Marketing, and Corporate and Other Operating. The Alumina segment mines for and purchases bauxite and other raw materials; refines bauxite into alumina; and sells alumina, as well as produces and sells refined alumina, gallium, and multi-form alumina bauxite. Its Primary Aluminum segment procures alumina and other raw materials, auxiliary materials, and electricity power; and produces and sells carbon, aluminum alloy, and other electrolytic aluminum products. The Energy segment mines for coal deposits; generates and sells electricity using thermal, wind, and solar power sources to regional power grid corporations; and manufactures power related equipment. Its Marketing segment trades in alumina, primary aluminum, aluminum fabrication products, other non-ferrous metal products, coal products, and raw and supplemental materials; and provides logistics and transport services. The Corporate and Other Operating segment provides research and development services; and engages in other aluminum-related business activities. The company is involved in the acquisition, manufacturing, and distribution of bauxite mines and limestone ore; engineering project; thermoelectric supply and investment management; and import and export activities, as well as manufacturing and distribution of anode and cathode carbon products. Aluminum Corporation of China Limited was incorporated in 2001 and is headquartered in Beijing, the People's Republic of China.

financial_summary: Aluminum Corporation of China L is a large-cap basic materials business with a $16.9B market cap on $43.3B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at +16% over the past three years, the kind of sustained demand persistence that marks a compounder.

Returns on capital run at 7% against a 8% cost of capital, which means the business is destroying value with every dollar it reinvests, and 8% gross margins are typical of commodity economics where competitors can replicate the product cheaply.

The business throws off $3.5B in free cash flow — roughly 8 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 2.56× so those profits are backed by real cash.
Accruals are elevated at -8.3% of assets, and Sloan showed firms building earnings through accruals rather than cash systematically underperform.
On the balance sheet, debt is moderate at 2.4× net debt/EBITDA, serviceable in normal conditions but worth watching through a downturn, and interest coverage runs at 4.2×.
Shareholder yield is only 0.5%, a thin return of capital, and insiders hold 9.1% of the shares, and profit capture is only 0.4× the fair share, suggesting no structural edge inside its industry.

sector_headwinds.text: Fragmented industry with below-average profit capture — no moat to protect margins
Volatile returns on capital suggest the moat is narrower than a snapshot ROIC implies
Altman Z in the grey zone — financial health warrants monitoring
Gross margin trails most Basic Materials peers — competitors appear to have the pricing hand
Cyclical sectors like Basic Materials tend to underperform in slowdowns
Late-cycle dynamics increase the probability of a slowdown
Commodity price volatility and cost-curve position — in a downturn only the lowest-cost producer has a business, and the rest carry the overhead.
Environmental remediation liability — tightening regulations on emissions, tailings, and water use create open-ended balance-sheet risk that grows with each legislative cycle.
Trade policy and tariff whiplash — materials producers are first-order casualties of protectionist swings, and margin gets squeezed from both input and output pricing.

sect: Its 6% operating margin is roughly in line with the Basic Materials median (10%).
It captures well under its share of sector profits (0.43x its revenue share).
It accounts for 2.6% of sector revenue and 1.1% of sector operating profit.
Over five years it has been gaining share of the sector profit pool (+2.5% a year).
The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.04 across 219 companies in the universe; the top four hold 25% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares are in a steep downtrend, down 33% over the past year excluding the latest month.
The price sits near the bottom of its 52-week range, 57% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 94% and a beta of 0.71, it is more defensive than the market, though its beta has shifted (1y 1.61 vs 5y 0.30), so read it loosely.
Trading is thin (about $3K a day), below the $1.0M liquidity floor flagged; building a position would move the price.
In past sell-offs it fell 51% in the 2020 crash, 61% in the 2022 bear market and 73% in 2008.
val: The stock trades 64% below its DCF fair value of $2.64, a meaningful margin of safety.
The fair-value models disagree (dispersion 31%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $1.95 to $3.61 (P10-P90), so treat the estimate as noisy.
On multiples it looks cheap against Basic Materials peers: P/E 5.5 vs 16.5, EV/EBITDA 1.3 vs 8.5 and P/FCF 4.9 vs 22.8 (sector median).
Against its own history it is dear: the EBIT multiple sits 38% above its 10-year median.
Earnings yields are mixed: an FCF yield of 20.6% (above the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 3.3% (vs the 8% bar).
The price implies 8.0% annual cash-flow growth, 13pp less than the model expects.
prof: ROIC of 7% falls short of the cost of capital of 8.0%, so growth at these returns destroys value; returns have swung a lot from year to year (CV 0.44).
It runs a 8% gross margin and converts 8% of revenue into free cash flow.
Earnings quality is mixed: a Piotroski score of 7/9 and cash conversion of 2.56x, but high accruals (-8.3% of assets).
ROE of 21% is amplified by 3.9x balance-sheet leverage (DuPont), so ROIC is the cleaner read on the business.
hlth: Leverage is moderate at 2.4x net debt to EBITDA ($2.6B of cash against $8.4B of debt), above the 1.5x gate, with interest covered 4.2x.
The current ratio of 0.87 means short-term liabilities exceed current assets.
growth: Revenue has compounded at 16.3% over 3 years and 10.2% over 5 years, so growth is accelerating, and it has been lumpy (year-to-year swings of 22%).
Free cash flow has compounded 40.5% a year over five years.
own: Insiders own 9.1%, meaningful skin in the game, and institutions hold 39%.
Shareholder yield is a modest 0.5% (6.4% in dividends).
people: With about 60,814 employees, each generates about $713K of revenue, in line with the Basic Materials median, and productivity has risen 10.2% a year.
That works out to $57K of free cash flow per employee.
Compensation governance scores well (3/10, lower is better).
